name: Lillooet
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: [p.84] The stress is phonemic, cf. mạ́qaʔ "snow" vs. mạqáʔ "poison onion" ... Moreover, the stress is mobile ... [p.88 §3] 1. The counting base for the distribution of the stress is (a) the (last) strong syllabifier in a word, or, if there is no strong syllabifier, (b) the first full syllabifier, or, if there is no full syllabifier, (c) the first weak syllabifier. 2. From this base the stress moves two syllabifiers at a time, as suffixes or clitics are added, as long as (a) it does not fall on the last syllabifier in a word, except when the last syllabifier is also the only full syllabifier ...; (b) it does not fall on a weak syllabifier (where it would, the weak syllabifier is ignored).
new_statements.citation: van Eijk, Jan P. 1981. "Stress in Lillooet." Papers for the XVI International Conference on Salish (and Neighbouring) Languages, pp. 84-90 (UBC lingpapers archive).
new_statements.locator: §1 Introduction p.84 and §3 'General stress-rule' p.88 (PDF sheets 1 and 3; two printed pages per sheet)
new_statements.rule_in_words: One primary stress per word (domain = word plus enclitics). The root carries a lexically located stress (phonemic minimal pairs; by default the first full vowel, but not always, e.g. qan̓ím). As suffixes/enclitics are added, stress shifts rightward in binary steps from that base (or from the last inherently stress-attracting 'strong' suffix), landing as far right as possible but never on the word-final syllabifier and never on a weak vowel (ə), which is counted but skipped; all-schwa words stress the first vowel; certain cluster consonants and C-shaped suffixes count as (weak) syllabifiers. Net effect: lexical/morphological base plus quantity(quality)-sensitive rightward alternating rhythm with non-finality.
new_statements.secondary_stress: van Eijk 1981 says nothing about secondary stress. Roberts 1993 (on file) reports that van Eijk treats secondary stress as entirely predictable and leaves it unmarked, and cites one fieldwork transcription with secondary stress on alternating syllables preceding the main stress (q'ʷəzq'ʷəzílx-kal̓áp type), i.e. trochaic alternation from the base.
new_statements.exceptions: §4 (p.88-89): roots in full vowel + glottalized resonant count as weak before a direct transitivizer; passive -əm is a full syllabifier and may take stress; -tam- is a weak syllabifier and is skipped; §2.2.2 suffix doublets (-ílx/-ləx etc.) depending on whether the suffix can receive stress; §5 enclitics are full syllabifiers regardless of shape, but a single clitic does not attract stress after an all-schwa word; strong suffixes (-ʔúl 'real', -cút reflexive, -úƛ̓) always attract stress, the second of two consecutive strong suffixes winning; fn.3 a few roots have stress on a weak vowel (papláʔ-type reduplications, mạqáʔ).
new_statements.domain_note: Explicitly the phonological word including enclitics ('The matrix for the distribution of the stress is therefore the word with enclitics (proclitics are irrelevant here)', p.84). Data are van Eijk's own fieldwork at Mount Currie (Lower/southern Lillooet) but the paper is framed for Lillooet as a whole.
new_statements.identity_note: van Eijk's 1981 data come from his Mount Currie fieldwork (Lower/southern Lillooet dialect, Lil'wat), though the paper is titled and framed for Lillooet generally; Roberts 1993 uses the same data. Swoboda 1971 and Davis's teaching grammar describe the Upper (Fountain/Fraser River) dialect. Glottolog lill1248 covers both dialects; no separate dialect glottocodes assigned here.

sources.note: Whole paper is on stress. p.84: one syllable per polysyllabic word is stressed; stress is phonemic (mạ́qaʔ 'snow' vs mạqáʔ 'poison onion', ƛ̓ámin 'fur' vs ƛ̓amín 'axe') and mobile (moves rightward as suffixes/enclitics are added; domain = word with enclitics). p.85: in all-full-vowel words stress moves two vowels at a time from the originally stressed one, never onto the last; 'first full syllabifier' = the stressed full vowel of the root (usually but not always the first, cf. qan̓ím). p.85-86: weak vowels (ə) are counted but cannot receive shifted stress; all-schwa words stress the first vow…

sources.citation: Roberts, Taylor. 1993. "Lillooet stress shift and its implications for syllable structure and prosody." Papers for the 28th ICSNL (Seattle), pp. 297-316.
sources.note: Analytic paper built entirely on van Eijk's data (cites van Eijk 1984:20-24 as the fuller description). p.297-298: 'stress can be seen to be unpredictable and contrastive in the following minimal pairs' (máqaʔ/maqáʔ); 'in root-suffix combinations, stress moves rightward two vowels at a time from the underlyingly stressed vowel of the root -- as far as possible -- as long as it does not fall on the last vowel of the word'; strong suffixes invariably attract stress. Analysis: left-to-right moraic trochees from the lexically stressed vowel, final-mora extrametricality, consonant clusters moraic;…
